domains.name: Practice Questions: Spark ML and Scaling

questions.title: Online vs Offline Feature Store Selection
questions.question: A recommendation model needs to return personalized results within 50ms of a user clicking a product page. Pre-computed user embeddings are updated nightly. Which feature store configuration is most appropriate?

choices.A: Offline feature store only — read feature values from Delta Lake at request time
choices.B: Online feature store — publish features to low-latency key-value store; model reads at serving time
choices.C: Recompute features from raw events inside the model serving endpoint
choices.D: Cache features in the driver node's memory between requests

questions.shortAnswer:
The online feature store is designed for sub-100ms serving latency. It holds a copy of features in a
low-latency store (a Databricks Online Feature Store on Lakebase, or a third-party store) so the serving endpoint can retrieve them
in single-digit milliseconds. Reading from Delta Lake (option A) incurs seconds of latency due to file
I/O and query planning, making it unsuitable for real-time serving requirements.

questions.title: Primary Key Requirement for write_table()
questions.question: A data engineer calls `FeatureEngineeringClient.write_table()` to persist a feature DataFrame to the feature store. The call raises a `MlflowException`. What is the most likely cause?

choices.A: The DataFrame contains null values in non-key columns
choices.B: The target feature table does not yet exist in Unity Catalog
choices.C: The DataFrame is missing the primary key column defined on the feature table
choices.D: The Spark session is not connected to a GPU-enabled cluster

questions.shortAnswer:
Every feature table in Databricks Feature Store requires a primary key. When `write_table()` is
called, the client validates that the DataFrame contains the primary key column(s) matching the
table's schema. If the primary key is absent or renamed, the write fails. Null values in non-key
columns are permitted, and the table can be created implicitly on first write if it does not exist.

questions.title: create_training_set() and lookup_key
questions.question: A data scientist uses `FeatureEngineeringClient.create_training_set()` with a `FeatureLookup` to join user features onto a label DataFrame. The label DataFrame has a column `user_id`. Which parameter on `FeatureLookup` connects the label DataFrame to the feature table?

choices.A: `join_key`
choices.B: `primary_key`
choices.C: `lookup_key`
choices.D: `entity_key`

questions.shortAnswer:
`FeatureLookup` uses the `lookup_key` parameter to specify which column(s) in the label DataFrame
correspond to the primary key of the feature table. If the column name in the label DataFrame
matches the primary key name on the feature table, `lookup_key` can be omitted — but when names
differ, it must be set explicitly. `join_key` and `entity_key` are not valid parameter names for
this API.

questions.title: Point-in-Time Correct Feature Retrieval
questions.question: A fraud detection model is trained on historical transactions. Each transaction has an `event_timestamp`. The data scientist wants to ensure that feature values joined to each transaction reflect only information available at the moment the transaction occurred, avoiding future leakage. Which parameter enables this in `FeatureLookup`?

choices.A: `feature_names` — list only features recorded before the event
choices.B: `timestamp_lookup_key` — specifies the column used for point-in-time correct joins
choices.C: `as_of_delta_version` — reads the Delta table version at the transaction time
choices.D: `max_lookback_days` — limits how far back in time features are retrieved

questions.shortAnswer:
Setting `timestamp_lookup_key` on a `FeatureLookup` instructs `create_training_set()` to perform a
point-in-time correct join: for each row in the label DataFrame, it retrieves the feature values
whose timestamp is the most recent one that does not exceed the value in `timestamp_lookup_key`.
This prevents future feature values from leaking into training data. The other options do not exist
as valid API parameters for this purpose.

questions.title: Feature Lineage via log_model()
questions.question: A team wants to track which feature table versions were used to train each model version, enabling them to reproduce training data for any registered model. Which method establishes this lineage automatically in Databricks?

choices.A: `mlflow.sklearn.log_model()` with `registered_model_name` set
choices.B: `FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model()` with the `training_set` parameter
choices.C: `mlflow.log_artifact()` with the feature table Delta log path
choices.D: `mlflow.set_tag("feature_table", table_name)` before logging the model

questions.shortAnswer:
`FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model()` accepts a `training_set` object (the output of
`create_training_set()`) and records the exact feature tables, primary keys, and feature names used
during training as part of the MLflow run metadata. This creates auditable lineage between every
model version and its source features. Using `mlflow.sklearn.log_model()` directly does not capture
feature store lineage.

questions.title: Automatic Feature Retrieval at Inference Time
questions.question: A model was logged with `FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model()` and deployed to a Databricks Model Serving endpoint. At inference time the client sends only `customer_id` in the request payload. How does the endpoint obtain the full set of feature values needed for prediction?

choices.A: The client must send all feature values in the request payload alongside `customer_id`
choices.B: The endpoint retrains a lightweight feature computation step on every request
choices.C: The model's pyfunc wrapper automatically retrieves features from the online store using `customer_id` as the lookup key
choices.D: A separate microservice must be called first to hydrate features before hitting the model endpoint

questions.shortAnswer:
When a model is logged via `FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model()`, Databricks packages a pyfunc
wrapper that knows which features to look up and from which feature tables. At serving time, the
wrapper uses the lookup key(s) from the request to fetch feature values from the online store and
assembles the full feature vector before calling the underlying model's predict function. This
eliminates the need for callers to know the feature schema.

questions.title: Train-Serving Skew Root Cause
questions.question: A production model shows higher error rates on live data than on the held-out test set, even though the input distribution has not shifted. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.A: The model was not registered in Unity Catalog before deployment
choices.B: The online feature store was not refreshed after training completed
choices.C: Feature values are computed differently between training (batch ETL) and serving (online lookup)
choices.D: The serving endpoint uses a different Python version than the training cluster

questions.shortAnswer:
Train-serving skew occurs when the feature engineering logic applied during training differs from
the logic used at serving time — for example, a mean imputation computed on the full dataset during
training versus a hardcoded constant at serving time. Even when the raw input distribution is
stable, inconsistent feature computation produces systematically different feature vectors, degrading
model accuracy. Using the Feature Engineering Client's `log_model()` and online store helps mitigate
this by ensuring the same feature definitions are used in both paths.

questions.title: publish_table() to an Online Store
questions.question: A team has a feature table stored in Delta Lake (offline store). They want to make those features available for sub-10ms lookups from a model serving endpoint. What is the correct next step?

choices.A: Copy the Delta table to a Parquet file on object storage accessible to the endpoint
choices.B: Call `FeatureEngineeringClient.publish_table()` to sync features to the online store
choices.C: Register the Delta table as an external table in Unity Catalog
choices.D: Mount the Delta table path as a DBFS mount accessible from the serving cluster

questions.shortAnswer:
`fe.publish_table(online_store=..., source_table_name=..., online_table_name=...)` pushes feature data from the offline Delta-backed store into the
online store (a Lakebase-backed Databricks Online Feature Store, or a third-party store), which supports single-digit millisecond
read latency required for real-time serving. The offline Delta table serves as the source of truth
for batch training, while the online store serves real-time inference. The other options do not
provide the low-latency key-value access pattern that serving requires.

questions.title: Feature Table Schema Requirements
questions.question: A data scientist attempts to create a feature table using `FeatureEngineeringClient.create_table()`. Which combination of requirements must be satisfied for the call to succeed?

choices.A: The table must have at least one primary key column and a numeric data type for all feature columns
choices.B: The table must have at least one primary key column; feature columns can be any supported Spark data type
choices.C: The table must have a composite primary key of exactly two columns
choices.D: The table must include a timestamp column alongside the primary key

questions.shortAnswer:
Databricks Feature Store requires at least one primary key column to enable feature lookups. Feature
columns themselves support any Spark SQL data type including strings, arrays, maps, and structs —
they are not restricted to numeric types. A timestamp column is optional and only needed when
point-in-time correct lookups are required. There is no requirement for a composite key.

questions.title: Creating a Training Dataset
questions.question: Which `FeatureEngineeringClient` method generates a training dataset by joining a label DataFrame with feature values from one or more feature tables?

choices.A: `get_training_set()`
choices.B: `join_features()`
choices.C: `create_training_set()`
choices.D: `build_dataset()`

questions.shortAnswer:
`create_training_set()` is the designated API for building a training dataset. It accepts a label
DataFrame, a list of `FeatureLookup` objects (specifying which feature tables and columns to join),
and optional parameters like `timestamp_lookup_key` for point-in-time joins. The returned
`TrainingSet` object can then be materialized with `.load_df()` or passed directly to
`log_model()`. None of the other method names (`get_training_set`, `join_features`,
`build_dataset`) exist in the Databricks Feature Engineering Client API.

questions.title: Delta Lake as the Offline Store
questions.question: A data engineer asks why feature data stored via `FeatureEngineeringClient.write_table()` supports time travel queries. What is the underlying reason?

choices.A: The Feature Engineering Client maintains a separate audit log table for each feature table
choices.B: Feature tables are backed by Delta Lake, which retains a transaction log and data file snapshots
choices.C: Databricks automatically creates a history table with `_HIST` suffix for every feature table
choices.D: The Feature Engineering Client snapshots feature values to DBFS on each write

questions.shortAnswer:
Databricks Feature Store uses Delta Lake as the underlying storage format for offline feature tables.
Delta Lake's transaction log records every write operation along with the data files associated with
each version. This means you can query any historical version of a feature table using `VERSION AS OF`
or `TIMESTAMP AS OF` syntax, which is foundational to point-in-time correct feature retrieval during
training.

questions.title: Online Store vs Passing Features Directly
questions.question: A batch scoring pipeline scores 10 million customer records nightly. Features are already computed and stored in a Delta table. A teammate suggests configuring the online store to serve these features. When is this suggestion necessary?

choices.A: Always — the online store is required for all model serving regardless of latency requirements
choices.B: Only when the serving endpoint must retrieve individual feature records in real time with low latency
choices.C: Only when the feature table exceeds 1 TB
choices.D: Only when Unity Catalog is not enabled

questions.shortAnswer:
The online store is designed for real-time, low-latency point lookups (single-digit milliseconds)
by entity key. For a nightly batch pipeline, the model can read features directly from the offline
Delta table using Spark — no online store is required. Publishing to the online store adds
operational complexity (cost, sync pipelines) that is only justified when individual records must
be retrieved in sub-100ms for interactive serving.

questions.title: Feature Sharing Across Teams with Unity Catalog
questions.question: Team A has created a feature table `catalog_a.features.customer_ltv`. Team B wants to use this feature table to train their own model. What must Team A do to enable this?

choices.A: Export the feature table to a shared DBFS path that Team B can read
choices.B: Grant Team B the appropriate privilege on the feature table in Unity Catalog
choices.C: Duplicate the feature table into Team B's catalog
choices.D: Convert the feature table to a view and share the view definition

questions.shortAnswer:
Feature tables stored in Unity Catalog are governed by UC's fine-grained permission model. Team A
can grant `SELECT` (and optionally `USE CATALOG` / `USE SCHEMA`) privileges to Team B's principal
(user, group, or service principal) without any data duplication. This is one of the key benefits
of Unity Catalog: centralized governance enables secure, auditable feature sharing across teams
within the same account.

questions.title: Avoiding Data Leakage with Point-in-Time Lookups
questions.question: A model predicts whether a customer will churn in the next 30 days. The training data contains churn labels from the past year. A data scientist joins customer activity features without using `timestamp_lookup_key`. What is the likely consequence?

choices.A: The join will fail because `FeatureLookup` requires a timestamp column
choices.B: All feature values will default to zero for historical rows
choices.C: Future feature values will leak into the training data, inflating model performance metrics
choices.D: The model will train correctly but fail to deploy due to a schema mismatch

questions.shortAnswer:
Without `timestamp_lookup_key`, `create_training_set()` uses the latest feature values for every
row in the label DataFrame, regardless of when each label was generated. For historical training
examples, this means features computed using data from the future (e.g., a customer's total logins
in the month after the label date) are incorrectly joined. This makes the model appear more accurate
during evaluation than it will be in production, a form of data leakage.

questions.title: Feature Versioning via Delta Table Versions
questions.question: A data scientist needs to reproduce the exact training dataset used to train model version 12, which was trained six months ago. The feature table has had many updates since then. How does Databricks enable this?

choices.A: The Feature Engineering Client stores a snapshot of every training dataset as a compressed artifact in MLflow
choices.B: Because feature tables are backed by Delta Lake, the model run's metadata records the Delta table version at training time, enabling `VERSION AS OF` queries
choices.C: Databricks automatically creates a read-only clone of the feature table for every `create_training_set()` call
choices.D: You must manually checkpoint the Delta table before each training run to enable later reproduction

questions.shortAnswer:
When `FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model()` is called with a `training_set`, Databricks records
the Delta table version(s) used for each feature table in the MLflow run's metadata. Because Delta
Lake retains its transaction log (subject to the configured VACUUM retention period), a data
scientist can reconstruct the exact feature DataFrame from six months ago by querying the feature
table `VERSION AS OF <recorded_version>`. This makes reproducibility a first-class concern in
the feature store design.

questions.title: Configuring an Online Table with the Databricks SDK *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A feature table `main.cx.customer_daily` holds one row per `(customer_id, snapshot_ts)` for the last two years. A Model Serving endpoint must look up the **latest** feature values per customer in milliseconds. Using the Databricks SDK, which online table specification meets the requirement?

choices.A: `OnlineTableSpec(source_table_full_name="main.cx.customer_daily", primary_key_columns=["customer_id"], timeseries_key="snapshot_ts", run_triggered=...)` created with `w.online_tables.create_and_wait(...)`
choices.B: `OnlineTableSpec(primary_key_columns=["customer_id", "snapshot_ts"])` with no time series key, so every historical row is served
choices.C: A SQL view that filters the Delta table to the latest snapshot, queried by the endpoint at request time
choices.D: `spark.read.table("main.cx.customer_daily").cache()` on the serving cluster

questions.shortAnswer: Primary key `customer_id` plus `timeseries_key="snapshot_ts"` keeps only the latest row per customer in the low-latency online copy.
questions.explanation:
Online tables are read-only, row-oriented copies of a Delta table that endpoints query by primary key. When the source holds history, the time series key tells the sync to keep the newest row per key. Option B would require callers to know the exact snapshot timestamp. A view or a cached DataFrame (C, D) isn't a low-latency serving store.

Platform note: legacy online tables became inaccessible after January 15, 2026. The current equivalent is `fe.create_online_store(...)` + `fe.publish_table(...)` (Databricks Online Feature Stores on Lakebase). Answer exam questions with the exam's online-table vocabulary.

questions.title: Triggered vs Continuous Online Sync *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A card-fraud model reads `txn_count_5m` from an online copy of a feature table. A Structured Streaming job updates the offline table every minute, and the business requires the endpoint to see new values within seconds. Cost is a secondary concern. How should the online sync be configured?

choices.A: Triggered sync scheduled hourly by a Lakeflow Job
choices.B: Continuous sync (`run_continuously` for an online table, or `publish_mode="CONTINUOUS"` for an online feature store)
choices.C: A one-time snapshot sync after each daily retrain
choices.D: No online copy. Recompute the 5-minute count inside the model's `predict()` from the raw event table

questions.shortAnswer: Continuous sync streams changes from the offline table to the online store with seconds of latency.
questions.explanation: Triggered sync is cheaper but only as fresh as the last trigger. Snapshot copies everything once. Recomputing aggregates from raw events in `predict()` adds latency and duplicates feature logic. When freshness in seconds is the requirement, continuous sync is the right trade-off. Triggered and continuous modes need Change Data Feed on the source table.

questions.title: On-Demand Features with FeatureFunction *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A model uses `amount_vs_7d_avg = amount / spend_7d`, where `amount` arrives with each request and `spend_7d` is a stored feature. The team wants identical computation in training, batch scoring, and Model Serving without duplicating code. What should they do?

choices.A: Compute the ratio in pandas in the training notebook, and have the calling application compute it before sending requests
choices.B: Register a Unity Catalog Python UDF, reference it with `FeatureFunction(udf_name=..., input_bindings=...)` next to a `FeatureLookup` in `fe.create_training_set`, and log the model with `fe.log_model(training_set=...)`
choices.C: Materialize the ratio nightly into the feature table so it can be looked up
choices.D: Add the ratio as a column in the inference table after scoring

questions.shortAnswer: `FeatureFunction` runs the same UC Python UDF at training time, in `score_batch`, and on the serving endpoint.
questions.explanation: Because the logged model carries the lookup and function metadata, Model Serving looks up `spend_7d` and runs the UDF per request. Callers send only keys and request-time columns. Option A duplicates logic (skew risk). Option C can't use a request-time value. Option D happens after prediction, so the model never sees the feature.

questions.title: Streaming Feature Computation with the FeatureEngineering Client *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A team computes 5-minute sliding-window aggregates with Structured Streaming and wants them written continuously to a Unity Catalog feature table through the FeatureEngineering Client. Which call is correct?

choices.A: `fe.write_table(name=..., df=streaming_df, mode="overwrite")` with no checkpoint
choices.B: `fe.write_table(name=..., df=streaming_df, checkpoint_location="/Volumes/.../ckpt", trigger={"processingTime": "1 minute"})`, which returns a `StreamingQuery`
choices.C: `fe.create_training_set(df=streaming_df, ...)` on every micro-batch
choices.D: Streaming DataFrames aren't supported; collect each micro-batch with `toPandas()` and call `write_table` in a loop

questions.shortAnswer: `write_table` accepts a streaming DataFrame, merges it into the feature table, and returns a `StreamingQuery`.
questions.explanation: `merge` is the only supported write mode, so `overwrite` (A) isn't valid. A checkpoint location makes the stream restartable, and the trigger defaults to a 5-second processing time. A watermark on the windowed aggregation bounds state. Options C and D misuse the API.

questions.title: Scheduled Feature Refresh with merge *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A nightly Lakeflow Job calls `fe.write_table(name="main.cx.customer_features", df=updates_df, mode="merge")`, where `updates_df` contains only customers who transacted yesterday. What happens to customers **not** present in `updates_df`?

choices.A: Their rows are deleted from the feature table
choices.B: Their feature values are set to NULL
choices.C: Their rows remain unchanged
choices.D: The call fails because `df` must contain every primary key

questions.shortAnswer: With `merge`, rows whose primary key isn't in the DataFrame stay unchanged.
questions.explanation: This makes incremental, automated feature pipelines cheap: each run upserts only the changed keys. Databricks recommends scheduling the feature notebook as a job for regular updates.

questions.title: SparkTrials vs Trials
questions.question: A data scientist wants to parallelize Hyperopt trials across a Spark cluster with multiple worker nodes. Which trials object should they use?

choices.A: `Trials()` — runs trials sequentially on the driver
choices.B: `SparkTrials()` — distributes trials across Spark executors
choices.C: `DistributedTrials()` — Hyperopt's built-in cluster mode
choices.D: `ParallelTrials(n_jobs=-1)` — uses all available cores

questions.shortAnswer: `SparkTrials` dispatches each trial to a Spark executor, enabling true distributed hyperparameter search across a cluster. `Trials` runs all evaluations sequentially on the driver node and is appropriate only for local, single-machine workloads. Options C and D do not exist in Hyperopt.

questions.title: fmin() Objective Direction
questions.question: A data scientist passes `roc_auc_score` directly as the objective function to `fmin()`. The search completes but the "best" model has the lowest AUC in the search. What is the problem?

choices.A: `fmin()` randomly selects the best trial rather than choosing by metric
choices.B: `fmin()` always minimizes the objective; returning raw AUC causes it to minimize AUC instead of maximizing it
choices.C: `roc_auc_score` is not a supported metric for Hyperopt
choices.D: The model was not serialized correctly during the trial

questions.shortAnswer: Hyperopt's `fmin()` treats the return value of the objective function as a loss to be minimized. To maximize AUC, the objective must return `1 - auc` or `-auc`. Returning the raw AUC score causes Hyperopt to search for hyperparameters that produce the lowest AUC, which is the opposite of the desired behavior.

questions.title: MLflow Autolog Run Structure with Hyperopt
questions.question: A data scientist enables `mlflow.sklearn.autolog()` and runs Hyperopt with `fmin()` for 20 trials. How are the MLflow runs organized?

choices.A: 20 independent top-level runs, one per trial
choices.B: 1 parent run containing 20 child runs, one per trial
choices.C: 1 run that logs all 20 trials' metrics in a single record
choices.D: 20 experiments, each containing one run

questions.shortAnswer: When `mlflow.autolog()` is active and an active MLflow run exists before `fmin()` is called, Hyperopt creates that run as the parent and nests one child run per trial beneath it. Each child run captures that trial's hyperparameters, metrics, and optionally the fitted model artifact. This hierarchy makes it straightforward to compare all trials under a single experiment entry.

questions.title: hp.loguniform vs hp.uniform for Learning Rate
questions.question: A data scientist needs to search learning rate values between `1e-5` and `1e-1`. Which Hyperopt search space expression is most appropriate?

choices.A: `hp.uniform('lr', 1e-5, 1e-1)`
choices.B: `hp.loguniform('lr', np.log(1e-5), np.log(1e-1))`
choices.C: `hp.quniform('lr', 1e-5, 1e-1, 0.001)`
choices.D: `hp.normal('lr', 1e-3, 1e-4)`

questions.shortAnswer: Learning rates span multiple orders of magnitude, so a log-uniform distribution is appropriate: it samples values such that ratios (e.g., 1e-4 to 1e-3) are as likely as (1e-2 to 1e-1). `hp.uniform` samples linearly and would overwhelmingly draw values near the upper end of the range, neglecting the small values that are often optimal. The arguments to `hp.loguniform` are `(label, low, high)` in natural-log space, so both bounds must be wrapped in `np.log()`.

questions.title: SparkTrials parallelism Parameter
questions.question: A data scientist sets `parallelism=8` in `SparkTrials(parallelism=8)`. What does this control?

choices.A: The number of Spark executor cores allocated to each trial
choices.B: The number of trials that run simultaneously across the cluster
choices.C: The total number of trials that will be evaluated
choices.D: The number of cross-validation folds run per trial

questions.shortAnswer: The `parallelism` argument in `SparkTrials` sets how many trials are dispatched to Spark executors at the same time. With `parallelism=8`, up to 8 trials are in flight concurrently. Higher parallelism increases throughput but can reduce the benefit of Bayesian search because fewer completed results are available to guide the selection of the next batch of trials.

questions.title: Early Stopping in Hyperopt
questions.question: A data scientist wants Hyperopt to stop automatically if no improvement is seen for 50 consecutive trials. Which approach is correct?

choices.A: Set `max_evals=50` in `fmin()` to cap total trials
choices.B: Pass `early_stop_fn=no_progress_loss(50)` to `fmin()`
choices.C: Use a `callbacks` argument with an `EarlyStopping` object
choices.D: Wrap `fmin()` in a try/except block and raise `StopIteration` after 50 flat trials

questions.shortAnswer: Hyperopt's `fmin()` accepts an `early_stop_fn` parameter for stopping conditions. The `hyperopt.early_stop.no_progress_loss(n)` helper returns a function that signals Hyperopt to stop when the best loss has not improved for `n` consecutive trials. Setting `max_evals` only caps the total count regardless of improvement. Hyperopt does not use a `callbacks` API or `StopIteration`.

questions.title: Bayesian vs Random Search for Limited Budgets
questions.question: A hyperparameter search space contains over 1,000 possible combinations. A team has a compute budget for only 50 trials. Which search strategy is most sample-efficient?

choices.A: Grid search — evaluates all combinations systematically
choices.B: Random search — unbiased sampling across the full space
choices.C: Bayesian optimization (TPE) — uses past trial results to guide future selections
choices.D: Manual search — a domain expert selects the 50 most promising configurations

questions.shortAnswer: Tree-structured Parzen Estimators (TPE), Hyperopt's default algorithm, builds a probabilistic model of the objective surface and focuses trials in regions likely to improve the result. With only 50 trials available out of 1,000+ combinations, this sample efficiency is critical. Grid search is infeasible at this scale, and random search is unguided. TPE consistently outperforms random search when the trial budget is small relative to the search space.

questions.title: hp.choice for Categorical Hyperparameters
questions.question: A data scientist wants Hyperopt to search over `["linear", "rbf", "poly"]` for an SVM kernel. Which Hyperopt space function should they use?

choices.A: `hp.uniform('kernel', 0, 3)`
choices.B: `hp.randint('kernel', 3)`
choices.C: `hp.choice('kernel', ["linear", "rbf", "poly"])`
choices.D: `hp.categorical('kernel', ["linear", "rbf", "poly"])`

questions.shortAnswer: `hp.choice` is the correct function for selecting one item from a discrete list of categorical values. It returns the selected element (e.g., `"rbf"`) rather than an index, so it plugs directly into model constructors. `hp.uniform` and `hp.randint` produce numeric values, not strings. `hp.categorical` does not exist in Hyperopt.

questions.title: CrossValidator parallelism in Spark ML
questions.question: A data scientist uses Spark ML's `CrossValidator` to perform 5-fold cross-validation over a parameter grid with 10 configurations, training 50 models total. What parameter controls how many models train simultaneously?

choices.A: `numFolds` — number of cross-validation folds
choices.B: `parallelism` — number of models to train in parallel
choices.C: `n_jobs` — standard scikit-learn parallel jobs argument
choices.D: `sparkContext.setParallelism(10)` — global Spark parallelism setting

questions.shortAnswer: Spark ML's `CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` both expose a `parallelism` parameter (default `1`) that specifies how many (model, fold) combinations are trained concurrently. Setting it to match the number of available executor cores significantly reduces wall-clock time for large grids. `n_jobs` is a scikit-learn concept not present in Spark ML. `numFolds` controls evaluation strategy, not concurrency.

questions.title: AutoML as a Baseline Before Manual HPO
questions.question: A team is beginning a new classification problem and needs the fastest path to a reasonable baseline model and starting hyperparameters. What should they do first?

choices.A: Run a random hyperparameter search with 100 trials using Hyperopt
choices.B: Manually tune a logistic regression as an interpretable starting point
choices.C: Run Databricks AutoML to generate a baseline notebook with hyperparameters automatically
choices.D: Train an ensemble of 10 default models and average their predictions

questions.shortAnswer: Databricks AutoML explores multiple algorithms and hyperparameter configurations, then generates an editable Python notebook containing the best model found along with the trial results. This gives teams a well-tuned starting point in minutes rather than hours. The generated notebook can then be used as a base for further refinement with Hyperopt. Running Hyperopt from scratch without a baseline risks spending budget on poorly structured search spaces.

questions.title: Hyperparameter Overfitting Risk
questions.question: A data scientist tunes hyperparameters by running 200 Hyperopt trials evaluated against the test set, selects the best configuration, and reports that test set AUC as the final model performance. What is the primary risk?

choices.A: Hyperopt cannot evaluate against a test set directly
choices.B: The reported AUC is optimistically biased because the test set influenced hyperparameter selection
choices.C: 200 trials is too few for reliable Bayesian optimization
choices.D: The model will underfit because hyperparameters were selected to minimize loss

questions.shortAnswer: When the test set is used to guide any model selection decision — including hyperparameter tuning — it is no longer a held-out, unbiased estimate of generalization performance. The correct practice is to tune on a separate validation set (or use cross-validation), and reserve the test set for a single final evaluation. Using the test set for HPO leads to overfitting to the test distribution and inflated performance estimates.

questions.title: Metrics Auto-Logged per Child Run
questions.question: With `mlflow.autolog()` enabled and Hyperopt running 20 trials using a scikit-learn model, what is logged in each child run?

choices.A: Only the hyperparameter values for that trial
choices.B: Only the final loss value returned by the objective function
choices.C: Model metrics, hyperparameter values, and the fitted model artifact
choices.D: Aggregate statistics across all 20 trials combined

questions.shortAnswer: When `mlflow.sklearn.autolog()` is active, each child run created by Hyperopt captures: the hyperparameter values passed to the trial, all metrics computed during `fit()` and `score()` (e.g., AUC, accuracy, RMSE depending on estimator type), and the fitted model serialized as an MLflow artifact. This makes each child run a complete, reproducible record of that trial. Aggregate analysis across trials is visible in the parent run.

questions.title: Distributing Optuna Trials with MLflow *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A team already uses Optuna on a single node. They want to spread trials across the executors of their multi-node Databricks cluster and have each trial recorded in an MLflow experiment, writing as little extra code as possible. What should they use?

choices.A: `optuna.create_study().optimize(objective, n_trials=200, n_jobs=32)`
choices.B: `MlflowStorage(experiment_id=...)` as the study storage and `MlflowSparkStudy(study_name=..., storage=...).optimize(objective, n_trials=..., n_jobs=...)`
choices.C: Hyperopt `fmin(..., trials=SparkTrials(parallelism=32))` with the Optuna objective unchanged
choices.D: Python `asyncio` tasks that each call `study.optimize` with an MLflow callback

questions.shortAnswer: `MlflowStorage` keeps the study in MLflow and `MlflowSparkStudy` runs trials on PySpark executors, logging each trial.
questions.explanation: Plain Optuna `n_jobs` (A) uses threads on the driver only. Hyperopt (C) is a different library with a different objective contract, and it's no longer shipped in Databricks Runtime ML after 16.4 LTS ML. Async tasks (D) don't distribute work across the cluster. `MlflowStorage` lives in `mlflow.optuna.storage` and `MlflowSparkStudy` in `mlflow.pyspark.optuna.study` (MLflow 3, pre-installed on Databricks Runtime 17.0 ML+).

questions.title: Starting Ray on a Databricks Cluster *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: An engineer wants to run a Ray Tune search across the workers of a classic Databricks cluster from a notebook. What must happen before the `tune.Tuner(...).fit()` call?

choices.A: Nothing. `ray.init()` alone automatically uses all Spark workers
choices.B: Start a Ray-on-Spark cluster with `ray.util.spark.setup_ray_cluster(...)`, then `ray.init()`
choices.C: Convert the cluster to serverless compute, which runs Ray natively
choices.D: Run `%pip install ray` after the Ray cluster starts, so workers pick up the library

questions.shortAnswer: `setup_ray_cluster` launches Ray worker nodes on the Spark cluster's executors. Ray then sees the whole cluster.
questions.explanation: Without it, `ray.init()` starts a local Ray on the driver only. Ray on Spark isn't supported on serverless-based runtimes. Running `%pip` on a running Ray cluster shuts it down, so install libraries first.

questions.title: Ray vs Spark for Distributing ML Work *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: Which workload is the **best** fit for Ray rather than Apache Spark on Databricks?

choices.A: Joining three Delta tables and aggregating them into a feature table
choices.B: Training a reinforcement-learning agent whose many simulation tasks have dynamic, heterogeneous resource needs
choices.C: Fitting a Spark ML logistic regression on 500 million rows already in Delta
choices.D: Running nightly SQL ETL to refresh gold tables

questions.shortAnswer: Ray excels at task (logical) parallelism: many independent, dynamic tasks such as RL, hyperparameter search, and deep-learning training.
questions.explanation: Spark excels at data parallelism, applying the same operation to every element of a large dataset: joins, aggregations, ETL, and MLlib. Databricks recommends combining them: Spark for the data-intensive stages, Ray for the compute-heavy stage.

questions.title: Structuring Nested Runs for Cross-Validated Tuning *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A data scientist evaluates 12 hyperparameter configurations with 5-fold cross-validation, then refits the winner on the full training set. They want configurations to be comparable in the MLflow UI and the final model traceable to the search. Which run structure fits best?

choices.A: One flat run per fold per configuration (60 runs) with tags for fold and configuration
choices.B: A parent run per fold, each with 12 child runs for the configurations
choices.C: A parent run for the search, one child run per configuration logging mean and std CV metrics, and a final-model run under the same parent for the refit
choices.D: A single run logging all 60 fold scores as separate metrics, plus the final model

questions.shortAnswer: Parent = search, children = configurations with aggregated CV metrics, plus a final-model run linked to the parent.
questions.explanation: This keeps the configurations side by side in the UI (one child each), stores the CV summary where it's compared, and links the final model to the search that produced it. Per-fold values can still be logged inside each child with `log_metric(..., step=fold)`. Flat runs (A) and fold-level parents (B) scatter each configuration's evidence; a single run (D) loses structure.

questions.title: Logging a Metric Series *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: During training, a team wants MLflow to chart validation loss for each of 50 epochs within one run. Which call should run inside the epoch loop?

choices.A: `mlflow.log_param("val_loss", loss)`
choices.B: `mlflow.log_metric("val_loss", loss, step=epoch)`
choices.C: `mlflow.set_tag("val_loss", loss)`
choices.D: `mlflow.log_dict({"val_loss": loss}, "loss.json")`

questions.shortAnswer: `log_metric` with `step` records a time series that the run page charts.
questions.explanation: Parameters are write-once inputs, tags are metadata strings, and `log_dict` saves a file artifact (each call with the same name would overwrite it). Only metrics with steps produce a per-epoch chart.

questions.title: Custom PyFunc with Request-Time Feature Engineering *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A custom `mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel` must derive `hour_of_day` and a ratio against a merchant lookup file from the raw request, then score with a scikit-learn estimator stored as an artifact. Where should each step go?

choices.A: Load the estimator and lookup file inside `predict()` on every call, so they're always fresh
choices.B: Load the estimator and lookup file once in `load_context()` via `context.artifacts[...]`; compute the features and score in `predict()`
choices.C: Compute the features in the client application and keep the model a plain `mlflow.sklearn` flavor
choices.D: Store the lookup file on the training cluster's local disk and read it by absolute path in `predict()`

questions.shortAnswer: `load_context()` runs once at load time for heavy artifacts; `predict()` runs per request for feature engineering and scoring.
questions.explanation: Packaging the transformation inside the model keeps training and serving consistent. Files passed through the `artifacts` dict are copied into the model package and resolved with `context.artifacts`. Local paths from the training cluster (D) don't exist on the serving container, and loading per request (A) adds latency.

questions.title: Unity Catalog Registry URI
questions.question: A data scientist registers a model using `mlflow.sklearn.log_model()` without calling `mlflow.set_registry_uri()` first. Where does the model get registered?

choices.A: Unity Catalog model registry, under the default catalog
choices.B: Workspace model registry (legacy), scoped to the current workspace
choices.C: The call fails with a `RegistryURINotSetError`
choices.D: A local MLflow tracking server on the driver node

questions.shortAnswer: When `set_registry_uri()` is not called, MLflow defaults to the workspace model registry (legacy; UC registry is current) (the legacy, non-UC registry). To target Unity Catalog, you must explicitly call `mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")` before registering models. The workspace registry uses stage-based promotion (Staging, Production) while the UC registry uses aliases.

questions.title: Model Alias URI Format
questions.question: A data scientist wants to load the model version tagged with the alias `champion` from a Unity Catalog registered model `ml_catalog.fraud.detector`. Which URI is correct?

choices.A: `models:/ml_catalog.fraud.detector/champion`
choices.B: `models:/ml_catalog.fraud.detector@champion`
choices.C: `models://ml_catalog/fraud/detector@champion`
choices.D: `uc://ml_catalog.fraud.detector:champion`

questions.shortAnswer: In Unity Catalog, model aliases are referenced with the `@` separator: `models:/<catalog>.<schema>.<model>@<alias>`. The three-part namespace replaces the simple model name used in the workspace registry. Option A uses a slash before the alias, which is the legacy workspace registry syntax for stage-based loading and is not valid for UC aliases. Options C and D use non-existent URI schemes.

questions.title: Legacy Stages in Unity Catalog
questions.question: A team migrates their model registry from the workspace registry to Unity Catalog. A developer calls `client.transition_model_version_stage(name, version, stage="Production")`. What happens?

choices.A: The model version is promoted to the Production alias in UC
choices.B: The call succeeds but the stage is stored as a tag rather than a true stage
choices.C: The call raises an error — UC does not support stage-based transitions; use aliases instead
choices.D: The model is copied to a separate production catalog automatically

questions.shortAnswer: Unity Catalog's model registry replaces the concept of stages (Staging, Production, Archived) with flexible, user-defined aliases. `transition_model_version_stage()` is a workspace-registry-only method and will raise a `MlflowException` when the registry URI is set to `databricks-uc`. The correct UC equivalent is `client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "champion", version)`.

questions.title: spark_udf result_type
questions.question: A regression model returns `float64` predictions. A data scientist loads it as a Spark UDF: `mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(spark, model_uri, result_type=???)`. What should `result_type` be?

choices.A: `"float"`
choices.B: `"double"`
choices.C: `"float64"`
choices.D: `DoubleType()`

questions.shortAnswer: The `result_type` parameter accepts Spark SQL type strings or `pyspark.sql.types` objects. Spark's `DoubleType` corresponds to the string `"double"`, which maps to Python/numpy `float64`. Using `"float"` would give `FloatType` (32-bit), losing precision. `"float64"` is a numpy dtype string, not a valid Spark type string. While `DoubleType()` (option D) also works, passing the string `"double"` is more concise and equally correct.

questions.title: load_model vs spark_udf Execution Location
questions.question: A team needs to score 50 million rows daily using an MLflow model. One option uses `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model()` followed by `model.predict(pandas_df)`. The other uses `mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf()` applied to a Spark DataFrame. What is the key architectural difference?

choices.A: `load_model` loads the model to each executor; `spark_udf` loads it only to the driver
choices.B: `load_model` runs inference on the driver node (single machine); `spark_udf` runs on executors (distributed)
choices.C: `spark_udf` requires a GPU cluster; `load_model` works on CPU clusters
choices.D: There is no meaningful difference — both use all available cluster resources

questions.shortAnswer: `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model()` returns a Python object used for prediction on the driver. For large datasets, the entire DataFrame must be collected to the driver, which is a bottleneck and may cause OOM errors at scale. `spark_udf` serializes the model to each executor and applies inference in parallel across partitions, making it the correct choice for scoring millions of rows efficiently.

questions.title: Scale-to-Zero Cold Start
questions.question: A Databricks Model Serving endpoint is configured with scale-to-zero enabled. A user sends the first request after the endpoint has been idle for two hours. What should they expect?

choices.A: The request fails with a 503 error and must be retried manually
choices.B: The request is fulfilled after a cold start while compute is provisioned and the model loads
choices.C: The request is served instantly from a cached model artifact on disk
choices.D: Scale-to-zero is not available on Databricks Model Serving

questions.shortAnswer: When scale-to-zero is enabled, the serving endpoint shuts down its compute when idle to reduce cost. The first request after an idle period triggers provisioning of new compute, loading the model into memory, and then serving the request — which adds noticeable cold-start latency. Databricks does not recommend scale to zero for production endpoints because capacity is not guaranteed while scaled to zero; latency-sensitive applications should disable it or keep minimum provisioned concurrency.

questions.title: Model Signature Enforcement
questions.question: A model is registered in MLflow with a signature requiring a `float` column named `age`. An incoming serving request sends `age` as a `string`. What happens at serving time?

choices.A: The serving endpoint silently coerces the string to float before inference
choices.B: The serving endpoint logs a warning but proceeds with inference using the raw string
choices.C: The serving endpoint returns a 400 error due to input schema validation failure
choices.D: The model ignores the signature at serving time; signatures are informational only

questions.shortAnswer: MLflow model signatures are enforced at serving time in Databricks Model Serving. When an incoming request does not match the expected input schema — wrong type, missing required column, or unexpected column — the endpoint returns an HTTP 400 (Bad Request) with a schema validation error message before the model ever runs inference. This protects models from unexpected input shapes that could cause silent failures or incorrect predictions.

questions.title: Traffic Split Totals
questions.question: A team configures a Model Serving endpoint with `champion` receiving 80% of traffic and `challenger` receiving 10%. What is the result?

choices.A: The remaining 10% is automatically routed to the default model
choices.B: The configuration is invalid — all traffic percentages must sum to exactly 100%
choices.C: The endpoint accepts the configuration and drops the unallocated 10% of requests
choices.D: The challenger receives the full remaining 20% at runtime despite the 10% configuration

questions.shortAnswer: Databricks Model Serving requires that the traffic split across all served model versions adds up to exactly 100%. If the total is less than or greater than 100%, the endpoint update is rejected with a validation error. To run an A/B test with champion at 80%, the challenger must be assigned the full remaining 20% to satisfy the constraint.

questions.title: Inference Table Configuration Timing
questions.question: A team launches a Model Serving endpoint without configuring inference table logging. Six months later they realize they need historical request and response data. Can they retroactively capture it?

choices.A: Yes — Databricks retains all inference data for 90 days and can backfill on request
choices.B: Yes — enabling inference tables at any point will back-populate from endpoint creation
choices.C: No — inference tables must be configured before deployment; retroactive logging is not possible
choices.D: No — inference tables are only available for endpoints using GPU compute

questions.shortAnswer: Inference table logging captures raw request payloads and model responses to a Delta table in real time. This logging must be configured when the endpoint is created or updated; Databricks does not retain historical payloads for later backfill. Teams planning to use inference data for monitoring, drift detection, or retraining should enable inference tables before going to production.

questions.title: Shadow Deployment
questions.question: In a shadow deployment, a challenger model runs alongside the champion. Who receives the challenger's predictions?

choices.A: 10% of real users, as a canary group
choices.B: Internal QA engineers only, via a separate API endpoint
choices.C: No users — the challenger runs in parallel but its predictions are logged only, not returned to callers
choices.D: All users, with results hidden unless they opt in

questions.shortAnswer: Shadow mode (also called shadow testing or dark launching) routes live production traffic to both the champion and challenger simultaneously. Only the champion's predictions are returned to users. The challenger's predictions are captured in logs or inference tables for offline comparison. This allows safety evaluation of the challenger on real traffic without any user-facing risk.

questions.title: Canary vs A/B Testing
questions.question: A team wants to detect whether a new model is statistically significantly better than the current champion at the same metric. Which deployment strategy is designed for this?

choices.A: Canary deployment — gradually increases traffic from 5% to 100%
choices.B: Shadow deployment — runs challenger in parallel with no user exposure
choices.C: A/B testing — splits traffic (typically 50/50) to enable statistical comparison
choices.D: Blue-green deployment — keeps both versions live and switches instantly on cutover

questions.shortAnswer: A/B testing deliberately splits traffic between champion and challenger (often 50/50) to collect comparable sample sizes for statistical hypothesis testing. The goal is to determine with confidence whether the performance difference is significant. Canary deployments roll out gradually (5% → 25% → 100%) to limit blast radius during release, not to run controlled experiments. Shadow deployments collect no user-observable signal because users only see the champion's output.

questions.title: Multi-Task Job run_if for Integration Tests
questions.question: A CI/CD pipeline is a Databricks multi-task job: Task A trains the model, Task B evaluates it against a gate threshold, and Task C runs integration tests. Integration tests should only execute if evaluation passes. How should Task C be configured?

choices.A: Set `depends_on: [B]` with no condition — tasks always run after dependencies complete
choices.B: Set `depends_on: [B]` with `run_if: ALL_SUCCESS` — only runs if Task B succeeded
choices.C: Set `depends_on: [A, B]` with `run_if: AT_LEAST_ONE_SUCCESS`
choices.D: Use a `try/except` block inside Task B to call Task C conditionally

questions.shortAnswer: Databricks multi-task jobs support `run_if` conditions on each task. `ALL_SUCCESS` means all upstream dependency tasks must have completed with a success status. If Task B (the evaluation gate) fails — because the model did not meet the threshold — Task C is skipped automatically. This is the standard pattern for conditional pipeline stages without needing custom control-flow code inside the tasks themselves.

questions.title: Promoting Challenger to Champion via Alias
questions.question: A challenger model (version 7) has passed all evaluation gates and must be promoted to the champion alias, replacing version 5. Which operation is correct?

choices.A: `client.delete_registered_model_alias(name, "champion")` then re-register version 7 as champion
choices.B: `client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "champion", 7)` — reassigns the alias to version 7
choices.C: `client.transition_model_version_stage(name, 7, stage="Production")`
choices.D: Delete version 5 from the registry, then the alias automatically moves to the latest version

questions.shortAnswer: In Unity Catalog, aliases are pointers that can be freely reassigned. Calling `set_registered_model_alias` with the same alias name and a new version number atomically moves the pointer from version 5 to version 7. The previous version (5) remains in the registry and is unaffected — it simply no longer holds the `champion` alias. No deletion is required, and `transition_model_version_stage` is a workspace-registry-only method.

questions.title: Custom pyfunc — When to Use PythonModel
questions.question: A team trains a model using an internal proprietary framework that MLflow does not have a built-in flavor for. They also need custom preprocessing steps bundled with inference. Which MLflow capability is appropriate?

choices.A: Use `mlflow.sklearn.log_model()` with a custom wrapper class
choices.B: Log the model weights as a generic artifact using `mlflow.log_artifact()`
choices.C: Implement `mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel` to create a custom MLflow flavor
choices.D: Write the model to Delta as a binary column and load it at serving time

questions.shortAnswer: `mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel` is MLflow's extension point for frameworks without a native flavor. By subclassing `PythonModel` and implementing `load_context()` and `predict()`, teams can bundle arbitrary model artifacts, dependencies, and pre/post-processing logic into a single deployable package. The resulting model is loadable via `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model()` and deployable to Databricks Model Serving like any other MLflow model.

questions.title: Drift-Triggered Retraining
questions.question: A Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring alert detects that the model's AUC on recent data has dropped below the threshold. Which retraining trigger type best describes this scenario, and what is the recommended mechanism to invoke retraining?

choices.A: Scheduled retraining — a cron job retriggers the training pipeline weekly regardless of performance
choices.B: Drift-triggered retraining — the monitoring alert fires a webhook that calls the Databricks Jobs API to start the training job
choices.C: Manual retraining — a data scientist reviews the alert and kicks off the pipeline by hand
choices.D: Event-triggered retraining — new data arriving in cloud storage automatically starts retraining

questions.shortAnswer: Drift-triggered (or performance-triggered) retraining responds to observed degradation rather than a fixed schedule, making it both timely and resource-efficient. Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring supports alert conditions on monitored metrics; when a threshold is breached, a notification can call a webhook that in turn invokes the Databricks Jobs REST API to start a retraining pipeline. This creates a closed-loop MLOps system where production monitoring directly drives model refresh.

questions.title: ML Assets as Code with Bundles *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A platform team wants the MLflow experiment, the Unity Catalog registered model, and the Model Serving endpoint for a churn model to be version-controlled and deployed identically to dev, staging, and prod with one command per environment. What should they use?

choices.A: Create the resources in the UI in each workspace and document the steps in a README
choices.B: Declare `experiments`, `registered_models`, and `model_serving_endpoints` resources in a bundle (`databricks.yml`) with one target per environment, and run `databricks bundle deploy -t <target>`
choices.C: Package the training code as an MLflow Project and run it in each workspace
choices.D: Submit one-off job runs with the Databricks CLI that create the resources if they don't exist

questions.shortAnswer: A bundle declares ML resources as configuration and deploys the same definitions to each target.
questions.explanation: Bundles (DABs in the exam guide; renamed Declarative Automation Bundles on March 16, 2026) support experiment, registered model (Unity Catalog), serving endpoint, job, pipeline, and quality monitor resources. Targets parameterize catalog names and workspaces. MLflow Projects package code, not workspace resources, and ad-hoc CLI runs aren't declarative.

questions.title: Deploy Code vs Deploy Models *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: In a regulated bank, data scientists can't access production customer data. Models must be retrained automatically each month on production data. Which deployment pattern fits?

choices.A: Deploy models: train in dev on a data sample and promote the artifact to prod
choices.B: Deploy code: promote reviewed and tested training code to prod, where the production pipeline trains on production data
choices.C: Train manually in prod notebooks each month
choices.D: Export production data to dev so the model can be trained there

questions.shortAnswer: Deploy code moves the code through environments and trains the final model in production.
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends deploy code in most situations. It suits restricted production data, and automated retraining is safer because the training code was reviewed and tested. Staging runs the same code on a limited subset as integration tests. Deploy models suits cases where training is very expensive or hard to reproduce.

questions.title: Organizing Functions and Unit Tests *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: Feature-transformation functions are used by several notebooks and must also be unit-tested automatically in CI on every pull request. Which organization does Databricks recommend for Python?

choices.A: Functions and their tests in the same notebook
choices.B: Functions in one notebook and tests in another notebook linked with `%run`
choices.C: Functions and tests in Python files in a Git folder or workspace files, imported by notebooks and run with `pytest`
choices.D: Functions copied into every notebook that needs them

questions.shortAnswer: Keep Python functions and their unit tests outside notebooks, in files.
questions.explanation: Files can be imported by notebooks and run by test frameworks in CI, and Databricks workspace tools can discover and run Python unit tests. The `%run` and same-notebook layouts are simpler, but those functions are hard to reuse and test outside notebooks. From a notebook, run `pytest.main([...])` and assert that the return code is 0 so failures fail the cell.

questions.title: Which Integration Tests to Re-Run *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: The ML pipeline has integration tests for feature engineering, training, evaluation, deployment, and inference. An engineer changes the **feature transformation** that computes `days_since_last_purchase`. Which integration tests must re-run at minimum?

choices.A: Feature engineering only
choices.B: Training and evaluation only
choices.C: Feature engineering, training, evaluation, deployment, and inference
choices.D: Deployment and inference only

questions.shortAnswer: A change re-tests its own stage and every stage downstream of it, and feature engineering is the first stage.
questions.explanation: New feature values change the training data, so the model must be retrained, re-evaluated, redeployed, and the inference path re-verified (including request-time feature logic). By contrast, a hyperparameter-only change starts at training and doesn't need the feature-engineering test re-run.

questions.title: Querying a Custom Model with an SDK *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A Python service must send records to a Model Serving endpoint named `churn-prod` and receive predictions. The team wants an SDK that handles authentication and payload formatting. Which call should they use?

choices.A: `mlflow.deployments.get_deploy_client("databricks").predict(endpoint="churn-prod", inputs={"dataframe_split": ...})`
choices.B: `mlflow.tracking.MlflowClient().get_run(...)` to read predictions from the latest run
choices.C: `requests.get(url + "?token=...&inputs=...")`
choices.D: `spark.sql("SELECT ai_query(...)")` from the Python service without a Spark session

questions.shortAnswer: The MLflow Deployments client's `predict()` takes the endpoint name and inputs, and handles auth and JSON formatting.
questions.explanation: Over raw REST, POST to `/serving-endpoints/<name>/invocations` with an `Authorization: Bearer` header and a JSON body such as `dataframe_split`. Never put tokens in the query string. The Tracking client doesn't call endpoints, and `ai_query` is a SQL function.

questions.title: Route Optimization on an Existing Endpoint *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A high-QPS fraud endpoint was created without route optimization. The team now wants its higher throughput and lower overhead latency. What must they do?

choices.A: Call `update_config` with `route_optimized=True` on the existing endpoint
choices.B: Create a new endpoint with `route_optimized=True`, move clients to its dedicated URL with OAuth tokens, then retire the old endpoint
choices.C: Enable route optimization in the AI Gateway settings of the existing endpoint
choices.D: Increase the workload size to Large, which turns on route optimization automatically

questions.shortAnswer: Route optimization can only be set when an endpoint is created.
questions.explanation: Route-optimized endpoints use a dedicated URL and accept only Databricks OAuth tokens, not personal access tokens. They're available for custom model and feature serving endpoints. Workload size controls concurrency, not routing.

questions.title: Safe Rollout on a High-Traffic Endpoint *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A payments-risk endpoint serves version 7 at high traffic. Version 8 is ready, and a bad model would be costly. Which rollout meets the requirement to minimize risk while keeping capacity?

choices.A: Replace version 7 with version 8 in a single config update at 100 % traffic
choices.B: Add version 8 as a second served entity at 5 % traffic, monitor errors, latency, and predictions, then raise its share step by step; set its share back to 0 % if checks fail
choices.C: Create a second endpoint for version 8 and ask half of the client teams to switch to it
choices.D: Enable scale to zero on version 7 so version 8 receives all new traffic automatically

questions.shortAnswer: A canary rollout through `traffic_config` limits the blast radius and allows instant rollback.
questions.explanation: During each config update, the existing configuration keeps serving traffic until the new one is ready, and a failed update leaves the active config in place. Size the served entities (workload size / concurrency) for peak traffic, and consider route optimization for throughput. After version 8 reaches 100 %, move the `@champion` alias in Unity Catalog.

questions.title: Blue-Green vs Canary *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: What distinguishes a blue-green deployment from a canary deployment for a model endpoint?

choices.A: Blue-green sends a small, growing share of traffic to the new version; canary switches all traffic at once
choices.B: Blue-green keeps two complete versions and switches all traffic at once, with fast switch-back; canary exposes the new version to a small share first and ramps up gradually
choices.C: Blue-green never exposes users to the new model; canary always uses 50 / 50 splits
choices.D: They're identical except for naming

questions.shortAnswer: Blue-green is an atomic switch with instant rollback; canary is gradual exposure.
questions.explanation: Blue-green needs capacity for both versions during cutover, and every user hits the new model at the switch. Canary limits impact to the canary share while you monitor, so it's the usual choice for business-critical, high-traffic endpoints. Shadow deployment, not blue-green, is the zero-exposure strategy.

questions.title: Registering a Custom PyFunc in Unity Catalog *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: An engineer logs a custom `PythonModel` that needs a tokenizer file at inference time and registers it as `main.nlp.intent_model`. Registration fails. What is the most likely fix?

choices.A: Register to the workspace registry instead; Unity Catalog doesn't accept PyFunc models
choices.B: Provide a model `signature` (or an `input_example` to infer it), set `mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")`, and pass the tokenizer through `artifacts={...}`
choices.C: Store the tokenizer in `/tmp` on the driver and read it from `predict()`
choices.D: Use a two-level name such as `nlp.intent_model`

questions.shortAnswer: Unity Catalog requires a signature, the UC registry URI, and a three-level name. Custom files go in `artifacts`.
questions.explanation: Files passed in `artifacts` are packaged with the model and resolved through `context.artifacts[...]` in `load_context()`, so they exist on the serving container. Once registered, the version can be deployed through the Serving UI, the REST API, or the Databricks / MLflow Deployments SDK.

questions.title: Data Drift vs Concept Drift
questions.question: **A model's input features have shifted distribution, but AUC remains stable at 0.93. Which drift type has occurred?**

choices.A: Concept drift — the model relationship changed
choices.B: Data drift only — input distributions changed but model still generalizes
choices.C: Prediction drift — outputs changed
choices.D: Label drift — target variable shifted

questions.shortAnswer: Data drift occurred (feature distributions shifted), but because AUC is stable, there is no concept drift. The model still correctly captures the input-output relationship despite the distribution change.

questions.title: PSI Threshold — No Action
questions.question: **A feature's PSI is calculated as 0.07. What is the recommended action?**

choices.A: Immediate retraining
choices.B: Investigate the data pipeline
choices.C: No action — within acceptable range (PSI < 0.10)
choices.D: Roll back to previous model

questions.shortAnswer: PSI < 0.10 indicates the population is stable. No immediate action is needed, though continued monitoring is recommended.

questions.title: PSI Threshold — Investigate
questions.question: **A feature's PSI score is 0.14 this week. What does this indicate?**

choices.A: No significant change — continue monitoring
choices.B: Slight population shift — investigate but retraining not yet mandatory
choices.C: Significant drift — retrain immediately
choices.D: Model is performing well

questions.shortAnswer: PSI between 0.10 and 0.20 indicates a slight but notable shift. Investigate the source of change; retraining may not be needed if model performance is unaffected.

questions.title: Chi-Square for Categorical Drift
questions.question: **A team monitors the `payment_method` feature (values: card, cash, wallet). Which statistical test detects distribution drift in this feature?**

choices.A: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
choices.B: Chi-square test
choices.C: t-test
choices.D: PSI with continuous binning

questions.shortAnswer: Chi-square test compares observed categorical frequencies to expected (baseline) frequencies. KS test requires continuous distributions.

questions.title: KS Test Applicability
questions.question: **A data scientist wants to detect drift in the `transaction_amount` feature (continuous, numeric). Which test is appropriate?**

choices.A: Chi-square test
choices.B: Fisher's exact test
choices.C: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
choices.D: Shapiro-Wilk test

questions.shortAnswer: KS test compares two continuous distributions and is the standard choice for detecting numeric feature drift.

questions.title: Lakehouse Monitoring Monitor Type
questions.question: **A team creates a monitor on an ML serving endpoint's inference table with prediction and label columns. Which monitor type should they select?**

choices.A: TimeSeries
choices.B: Snapshot
choices.C: InferenceLog
choices.D: DriftProfile

questions.shortAnswer: InferenceLog is the specialized monitor type for ML inference tables. It computes model performance metrics (accuracy, AUC, RMSE) in addition to drift metrics.

questions.title: Baseline Table Requirement
questions.question: **Why does Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring require a baseline table when computing drift metrics?**

choices.A: Drift is always compared against the previous day's data
choices.B: Drift metrics compare the current window's statistics against the baseline — without it, no relative comparison is possible
choices.C: The baseline table stores model hyperparameters
choices.D: Databricks uses the baseline to retrain models automatically

questions.shortAnswer: LHM computes drift by comparing the current monitoring window's profile against the baseline table (typically training data or an established reference period).

questions.title: Inference Table Timing
questions.question: **A model goes to production on Monday without inference tables configured. On Thursday the team enables inference tables. Which requests are captured?**

choices.A: All requests from Monday onward
choices.B: Only requests from Thursday onward
choices.C: Requests from the past 7 days are backfilled
choices.D: Requests from the past 24 hours are backfilled

questions.shortAnswer: Inference tables are prospective only. They capture requests after configuration; retroactive logging of past traffic is not possible.

questions.title: UC Audit Logs Location
questions.question: **A compliance team needs to audit all MLflow model alias changes over the past 30 days. Where should they query?**

choices.A: `system.runtime.query_history`
choices.B: `system.access.audit` table
choices.C: `mlflow.runs` experiment table
choices.D: Databricks model serving logs

questions.shortAnswer: Unity Catalog audit events including `updateModelVersionAlias` are logged to `system.access.audit` in UC-enabled workspaces.

questions.title: SHAP for Regulatory Compliance
questions.question: **A financial institution must explain why a specific loan application was denied by an ML model. Which technical control satisfies GDPR Article 22's right to explanation?**

choices.A: Show the model's overall accuracy
choices.B: Show the model version number and training date
choices.C: Provide SHAP values showing each feature's contribution to the denial decision
choices.D: Show the prediction probability score only

questions.shortAnswer: SHAP values provide local, instance-level explanations showing which features drove the prediction. This satisfies the "meaningful information about the logic involved" requirement of GDPR Article 22.

questions.title: Disparate Impact Rule
questions.question: **A credit scoring model has an approval rate of 65% for Group A and 84% for Group B. What is the disparate impact ratio and what does it indicate?**

choices.A: 0.77 — below the four-fifths (0.80) threshold, indicates potential discrimination
choices.B: 0.77 — above the minimum threshold, no concern
choices.C: 1.29 — above 1.0, model is biased toward Group B
choices.D: 0.65 — the minority group's raw approval rate

questions.shortAnswer: Disparate impact = 65% / 84% = 0.774. This is below the four-fifths rule threshold of 0.80, indicating potential discriminatory impact requiring investigation.

questions.title: UC EXECUTE Permission
questions.question: **A serving endpoint service principal needs to load and serve a model from `ml_catalog.fraud_models.fraud_classifier`. Which permission is required?**

choices.A: `SELECT ON MODEL`
choices.B: `MODIFY ON MODEL`
choices.C: `EXECUTE ON MODEL`
choices.D: `USE CATALOG`

questions.shortAnswer: `EXECUTE ON MODEL` grants the right to load and serve a model. `MODIFY` allows registering versions and setting aliases, but not serving.

questions.title: Prediction Drift as Proxy
questions.question: **Ground truth labels are available only after 14 days. What monitoring approach detects potential model degradation before labels arrive?**

choices.A: Wait 14 days and compute AUC retroactively
choices.B: Monitor prediction score distributions for drift using PSI
choices.C: Disable monitoring until labels arrive
choices.D: Use the model's training metrics as the current performance estimate

questions.shortAnswer: Prediction drift (monitoring output distribution changes) serves as a leading indicator. Significant PSI on prediction scores often precedes measurable AUC degradation once labels arrive.

questions.title: Feature Importance Drift
questions.question: **A team suspects that some features have become less informative in production compared to training. How should they investigate?**

choices.A: Compare training AUC vs production AUC
choices.B: Compare mean absolute SHAP values from training vs production data
choices.C: Re-run hyperparameter optimization
choices.D: Check the feature table's Delta version

questions.shortAnswer: Comparing SHAP value distributions between training and production data reveals which features have changed importance. A feature that was highly important during training but has low SHAP values in production indicates distribution shift in that feature.

questions.title: Concept Drift Detection Requirement
questions.question: **Which of the following is REQUIRED to detect concept drift (not just data drift)?**

choices.A: Feature distribution statistics from production
choices.B: Model training logs from MLflow
choices.C: Ground truth labels from production
choices.D: SHAP values from the model

questions.shortAnswer: Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the target has changed. Detecting it requires comparing predictions against actual outcomes (ground truth). Without labels, you can only detect data drift or prediction drift.

questions.title: Reading Categorical Drift from the Drift Metrics Table *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A Lakehouse Monitoring profile tracks `merchant_category`, a string column. Which drift-metrics-table columns hold meaningful values for this column?

choices.A: `ks_test` and `wasserstein_distance`
choices.B: `population_stability_index` only
choices.C: `chi_squared_test`, `tv_distance`, `l_infinity_distance`, and `js_distance`
choices.D: None. Categorical columns aren't profiled

questions.shortAnswer: Categorical columns get chi-square, total variation, L-infinity, and Jensen–Shannon statistics.
questions.explanation: `ks_test`, `wasserstein_distance`, and `population_stability_index` apply to numeric columns only and are NULL for categorical columns. Pair the chi-square p-value (significance) with a distance such as JS or TV (magnitude) before deciding to act.

questions.title: Baseline vs Consecutive Drift *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A team wants to know (1) whether this week's feature distributions differ from the training data, and (2) whether they changed suddenly compared with last week. How do they get both from Lakehouse Monitoring?

choices.A: Only (2) is possible. Monitors can't compare against training data
choices.B: Set `baseline_table_name` to the training data; read `drift_type = 'BASELINE'` rows for (1) and `drift_type = 'CONSECUTIVE'` rows for (2)
choices.C: Create two monitors on the same table, one per comparison
choices.D: Use `slicing_exprs` with the value `baseline`

questions.shortAnswer: `BASELINE` drift compares to the baseline table; `CONSECUTIVE` drift compares each window to the previous one.
questions.explanation: Without a baseline table, only consecutive drift is computed. Only one profile can exist per table, and slicing expressions split the data by segment; they don't define comparisons.

questions.title: Choosing a Profile Type *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A `dim_customer` table has no event timestamp and is fully rewritten each night. The team wants to track null rates and distributions of the whole table over time. Which profile type fits?

choices.A: InferenceLog
choices.B: TimeSeries
choices.C: Snapshot
choices.D: No profile is possible without a timestamp column

questions.shortAnswer: Snapshot profiles the full table contents at each refresh.
questions.explanation: TimeSeries and InferenceLog need a timestamp column for windows. InferenceLog adds model-quality metrics for prediction tables. Snapshot profiles are limited to 4 TB; use TimeSeries for larger tables.

questions.title: Custom Metric Types *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A fraud team wants (1) the total dollar amount of missed fraud per window, computed from table columns, and (2) how much that amount changed versus the baseline. Which custom metric types do they need?

choices.A: (1) derived, (2) aggregate
choices.B: (1) aggregate, (2) drift
choices.C: (1) drift, (2) derived
choices.D: Both aggregate

questions.shortAnswer: Aggregate metrics compute from table columns into the profile metrics table; drift metrics compare them across windows or against the baseline into the drift metrics table.
questions.explanation: Derived metrics combine previously computed aggregate metrics without scanning the table. Drift definitions use templates such as `{{current_df}}.metric - {{base_df}}.metric`. Custom metrics are defined with `MonitorMetric` / `MonitorMetricType` and passed as `custom_metrics`.

questions.title: Per-Segment Monitoring *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A model's overall accuracy is stable, but the team suspects it degrades for transactions above $1,000 and for some merchant categories. How should the monitor be configured to show this?

choices.A: Add `slicing_exprs=["amount > 1000", "merchant_category"]`
choices.B: Add `granularities=["1 hour"]`
choices.C: Create a separate table per merchant category
choices.D: Lower the alert threshold on overall accuracy

questions.shortAnswer: Slicing expressions compute every metric per slice: true / false for a predicate, and one slice per value for a column.
questions.explanation: Rows with `slice_key IS NULL` cover the whole table. High-cardinality columns slice on their top 100 values. Granularities change window sizes, not segments.

questions.title: Monitoring Endpoint Health *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: An SRE team needs alerts when a custom model endpoint's p95 latency, 5xx error rate, CPU usage, or memory usage spikes, in their existing Prometheus / Datadog stack. Where do these signals come from?

choices.A: The Lakehouse Monitoring drift metrics table
choices.B: Model Serving endpoint metrics: shown in the Serving UI and exported through `/api/2.0/serving-endpoints/{name}/metrics` for Prometheus or Datadog scraping
choices.C: The MLflow experiment of the training run
choices.D: `system.access.audit`

questions.shortAnswer: Model Serving exposes infrastructure metrics (latency, request rate, error rate, CPU, memory) and a metrics export API.
questions.explanation: The Serving UI shows them for the last 14 days by default.
