Exported metrics include `request_latency_ms`, `request_5xx_count_total`, `cpu_usage_percentage`, and `mem_usage_percentage`. Profile and drift tables describe data and model quality, not infrastructure health. Inference tables can supplement latency and status codes for long-term history.

questions.title: Selection Metric for Threshold-Driven Decisions *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: An insurer auto-approves claims when the model's predicted probability of legitimacy is at least 0.9, auto-rejects at 0.1 or below, and sends the rest to manual review. Which metric should automated retraining use to select the best candidate model?

choices.A: Accuracy
choices.B: AUROC
choices.C: Log loss
choices.D: Recall of the positive class

questions.shortAnswer: Actions depend on calibrated probabilities, and log loss directly penalizes poorly calibrated probabilities.
questions.explanation: AUROC measures ranking, and accuracy and recall evaluate hard labels at one threshold. A model can rank well yet be over-confident near 0.9, which is exactly where decisions happen. Compare challenger and champion on the same hold-out set, and require a minimum improvement plus guardrails before promotion.

questions.title: Automating Retraining from Monitoring *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A team wants retraining to start automatically when a monitored model's `log_loss` in the profile metrics table exceeds a threshold. Which design implements this on Databricks?

choices.A: Wait for a data scientist to notice the dashboard and run the training notebook
choices.B: Schedule the monitor refresh, then run a job whose first task queries the metric table and fails or exits when the threshold isn't breached, gating a downstream retraining task (or use a SQL alert that triggers the job)
choices.C: Set the endpoint's workload size to Large so it retrains itself
choices.D: Enable inference tables, which retrain the model when drift is detected

questions.shortAnswer: A metric-check task (or alert) on the monitor's tables gates or triggers the retraining job.
questions.explanation: The Declarative Automation Bundles docs show this pattern: a `quality_monitors` resource plus a retraining job whose first task checks a monitored metric for violations. The retrained model then passes an evaluation gate before alias promotion. Inference tables only log requests; they don't retrain anything.

questions.title: When Spark ML Is Recommended *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: Which scenario most clearly calls for Spark ML rather than scikit-learn on the driver?

choices.A: A 40 MB CSV with 20,000 rows for a quick prototype
choices.B: A 900-million-row Delta table of telemetry, where the training pipeline must keep working as volume grows
choices.C: A model that needs a transformer-based deep-learning architecture
choices.D: A single-record, sub-20 ms real-time scoring API

questions.shortAnswer: Data far larger than one machine's memory, already in Delta and still growing, is the Spark ML signal.
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends single-machine training when data and model fit in memory, because distributed code adds complexity and communication overhead. Deep learning belongs with TorchDistributor or Ray, and single-record real-time scoring favors a single-node model on Model Serving.

questions.title: Estimators vs Transformers *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: In the pipeline `[StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler, RandomForestClassifier]`, which stage does **not** learn anything from the training data?

choices.A: `StringIndexer`
choices.B: `OneHotEncoder`
choices.C: `VectorAssembler`
choices.D: `RandomForestClassifier`

questions.shortAnswer: `VectorAssembler` is a pure transformer: it concatenates columns into one vector.
questions.explanation: `StringIndexer` learns the category-to-index mapping, `OneHotEncoder` learns category sizes (it's an estimator since Spark 3.0), and the classifier learns model parameters. All three are fitted when `Pipeline.fit()` runs, which returns a `PipelineModel`.

questions.title: Building a Pipeline for Mixed Features *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A 300-million-row dataset has numeric columns (`income`, `tenure`) and string columns (`plan_type`, `region`). The team will train a logistic regression and wants preprocessing to scale with the data. Which pipeline is correct?

choices.A: `VectorAssembler` on all four columns → `LogisticRegression`
choices.B: `StringIndexer` on the string columns → `OneHotEncoder` on the indexes → `VectorAssembler` on the numeric and encoded columns → `LogisticRegression`
choices.C: `pandas.get_dummies` on a `toPandas()` copy → `LogisticRegression`
choices.D: `OneHotEncoder` directly on the string columns → `LogisticRegression`

questions.shortAnswer: Index the strings, one-hot encode the indexes, assemble one feature vector, then fit the estimator.
questions.explanation: `VectorAssembler` can't take raw string columns, and Spark's `OneHotEncoder` expects numeric category indexes, so `StringIndexer` must come first. Linear models need one-hot vectors so that indexes don't imply an order. `toPandas()` on 300 million rows doesn't scale.

questions.title: Estimator for a Continuous Target *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A logistics team predicts delivery time in minutes from distance, weather, and traffic features. Which Spark ML estimator fits the task?

choices.A: `LogisticRegression`
choices.B: `NaiveBayes`
choices.C: `GBTRegressor`
choices.D: `MultilayerPerceptronClassifier`

questions.shortAnswer: A continuous target is a regression problem, so use a regressor such as `GBTRegressor` or `LinearRegression`.
questions.explanation: Logistic regression, Naive Bayes, and the multilayer perceptron classifier all predict classes despite their names. Evaluate regressors with `RegressionEvaluator` (`rmse`, `mae`, `r2`).

questions.title: CrossValidator vs TrainValidationSplit *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: Tuning a Spark ML pipeline over 24 parameter combinations on a 2-billion-row table with 5-fold `CrossValidator` is too slow. Which change keeps a principled validation step at much lower cost?

choices.A: Replace `CrossValidator` with `TrainValidationSplit(trainRatio=0.8)`
choices.B: Raise `numFolds` to 10 for a more stable estimate
choices.C: Evaluate on the training data instead of a validation split
choices.D: Remove the evaluator and pick the last parameter map

questions.shortAnswer: `TrainValidationSplit` fits each combination once instead of k times.
questions.explanation: With very large data, one validation split is usually reliable enough, and it cuts cost by roughly the number of folds. `parallelism` controls how many combinations fit at once, so set it to what the cluster can handle. Evaluating on training data hides overfitting.

questions.title: Scoring a Streaming Source *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A registered Spark ML `PipelineModel` must score records continuously as they land in a Delta table. What is the simplest correct approach?

choices.A: Retrain a separate streaming model, because batch models can't score streams
choices.B: Load it with `mlflow.spark.load_model(...)` and call `.transform()` on `spark.readStream.table(...)`, writing with `writeStream` and a checkpoint location
choices.C: Collect each micro-batch to the driver and call `predict` row by row
choices.D: Deploy the model to a REST endpoint and call it once per row from a Python loop

questions.shortAnswer: A fitted `PipelineModel` transforms streaming DataFrames with the same `transform()` call it uses for batch.
questions.explanation: Write the scored stream to Delta with a checkpoint so it can restart. `mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf` is an alternative that works for any MLflow model, including single-node ones. Per-row REST calls or driver collection don't scale.

questions.title: Model Choice for Real-Time Inference *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A checkout service needs a fraud score for one transaction at a time within 30 ms. The current model is a Spark ML `PipelineModel`. Which approach best fits the latency requirement?

choices.A: Keep the Spark ML model and score each request with a Spark job on an all-purpose cluster
choices.B: Train an equivalent single-node model (for example scikit-learn or XGBoost) and serve it on a Model Serving endpoint
choices.C: Score all possible transactions nightly in batch
choices.D: Run Structured Streaming with a 1-second trigger and have the service poll the output table

questions.shortAnswer: For single-record, millisecond scoring, a single-node model on Model Serving avoids Spark overhead.
questions.explanation: Spark's parallelism pays off across many rows, not inside one request. Outside a cluster, MLflow's Spark flavor has to instantiate a SparkContext to score, which adds latency. Batch and streaming fit throughput workloads, not synchronous per-request answers.

questions.title: Group-Specific Training with applyInPandas *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A retailer needs a separate demand model for each of 3,000 stores, trained in parallel on the cluster. Which approach is correct?

choices.A: Loop over the stores on the driver, calling `toPandas()` and training each model in turn
choices.B: `df.groupBy("store_id").applyInPandas(train_fn, schema="store_id string, rmse double, run_id string")`, where `train_fn` takes and returns a pandas DataFrame
choices.C: `df.mapInPandas(train_fn, schema)` with no grouping
choices.D: One Spark ML model with `store_id` one-hot encoded

questions.shortAnswer: Grouped map (`applyInPandas`) hands each store's rows to `train_fn` as a pandas DataFrame and runs the groups in parallel.
questions.explanation: The returned DataFrame must match the declared schema. Pass the experiment and parent run IDs into the function explicitly if each group logs a child run to MLflow, because executors don't see the driver's active run. `mapInPandas` doesn't guarantee that a store's rows arrive together.

questions.title: applyInPandas Out-of-Memory on One Group *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: An `applyInPandas` training job succeeds for 2,999 stores but fails with out-of-memory errors on the flagship store, which has 60× more rows than average. What is the cause, and what fixes it?

choices.A: `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch` is too high; lowering it splits the group
choices.B: All of a group's data is loaded into memory at once; split or salt the oversized key, pre-aggregate, or give executors more memory
choices.C: `applyInPandas` can't process more than 1 GB in total; switch to a pandas UDF
choices.D: The output schema is wrong

questions.shortAnswer: Each group must fit in executor memory, because all of its rows are loaded before the function runs.
questions.explanation: `maxRecordsPerBatch` doesn't apply to groups, so tuning it doesn't help. Skewed keys are the usual cause. Split them into sub-groups, reduce the data per group, or increase executor memory.

questions.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A team trains a gradient-boosting model on 6 GB of tabular data. Training takes 40 minutes on a small node, and they want it faster with minimal code changes. What should they try first?

choices.A: Rewrite the training in Spark ML and add 20 workers
choices.B: Scale vertically: use a larger single node (more cores and memory) with the same single-node library
choices.C: Port the model to Ray Train across 50 nodes
choices.D: Split the data into shards and average models trained separately

questions.shortAnswer: When data and model fit on one machine, scaling up is the simplest and usually the most efficient option.
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends single-machine training when possible. Horizontal scaling adds distributed code and communication overhead, and it's worth it when data or model no longer fit, or when the work is many independent tasks such as tuning trials.

questions.title: Data vs Model Parallelism *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: A team fine-tunes a deep-learning model whose parameters, gradients, and optimizer state don't fit in one GPU's memory, on a multi-GPU node. Which strategy fits?

choices.A: Plain DDP (Distributed Data Parallel), which keeps a full model replica on every GPU
choices.B: Sharded data parallelism or model parallelism, for example FSDP or DeepSpeed ZeRO, which shard model state across GPUs
choices.C: Hyperparameter tuning with more trials
choices.D: `applyInPandas` grouped by GPU ID

questions.shortAnswer: When the model doesn't fit on one device, shard the model state (FSDP / ZeRO) or split the model (pipeline / tensor parallelism).
questions.explanation: DDP replicates the full model on each GPU, so it suits models that fit on one GPU and need more data throughput. Databricks' multi-GPU guidance maps DDP to the case where the model fits, and FSDP / DeepSpeed ZeRO to very large models.

questions.title: Comparing Ray and Spark *(2026 guide)*
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares Ray and Spark on Databricks?

choices.A: Ray replaces Spark for ETL and SQL on Databricks
choices.B: Spark excels at data parallelism (the same operation over a large dataset); Ray excels at task parallelism (many independent or dynamic tasks such as tuning trials and RL); they can run together on one cluster
choices.C: Ray runs only on serverless compute, and Spark only on classic clusters
choices.D: Spark can't train ML models; only Ray can

questions.shortAnswer: Use Spark for data-intensive stages and Ray for compute-intensive, task-parallel stages.
questions.explanation: Ray on Databricks runs on Spark clusters (`setup_ray_cluster`). It isn't supported on serverless-based runtimes; Ray on AI Runtime covers serverless GPU. Spark ML trains distributed models at data scale.
